source_title: 30 Years Later, Scream Has a Problem Its Sequels Can't Fix
source_excerpt:
Horror movies often channel the fears and anxieties society holds at the time of their release. The '90s were no exception, and many of the films from that decade say a lot about how filmmakers were interpreting and predicting the world's then-current direction. In 1996, writer Kevin Williamson tapped into the vapid culture of tabloid television prevalent in that era, and the potential impact of the media landscape on teens. The result was Scream , which redefined the slasher genre for the '90s. The movie's killers were Billy Loomis and Stu Macher, a pair of Woodsboro High School students who were just as scary when they took off the Ghostface costume.
Stu and Billy are vital to the original Scream , not just as characters who exist in its world, but also in its themes. And it all fits together because there are clear hints that the two are conspiring very early on. However, only at Scream 's climax do audiences learn about their dual roles as Ghostface, alongside their motives. The two planned on killing everyone, blaming Sidney Prescott's father for the crimes, and continuing as survivors to plan "sequels" to their movie-inspired massacre. Billy's reasoning is also partly based on revenge, but their motivations are key to understanding everything that came before. The problem is that the series has almost completely failed to replicate this model.
How Ghostface is Different From Every Other Horror Icon
Things started to unravel with Scream 2 . The sequel began a trend where Ghostface would return (alongside voice actor Roger L. Jackson), with new killers behind the mask. That distinguished the villain from classic horror icons like Freddy Krueger and Michael Myers, but it also caused a unique problem. As the series has progressed across three decades, the whodunnit aspect that popularized the original Scream remained unchanged. Unfortunately, few entries have delivered a satisfying reveal that connects with the themes or plot. Instead, the killers have become increasingly forgettable, while their motivations have also become increasingly contrived. As a result, it's almost impossible for the audience to feasibly guess the culprits before the climax.
We got a surprise for you, Sidney! Yeah, you're gonna love this one. It's a SCREAM, baby!
Part of the problem is that it seems like the writers are struggling to come up with new enemies for Sidney Prescott to deal with. Bringing back Ghostface in a new Scream movie is a lot more complicated to explain than outlining why Jason Voorhees came back to threaten Camp Crystal Lake. At this point, the Scream series has made a previous killer's parent the culprit in multiple Scream movies. In its own way, it almost seems less plausible that new people would keep taking up the Ghostface mantle than it is that lightning resurrected Jason's corpse in a Friday the 13th movie.
This lack of originality was on full display in 2026's Scream 7 . The killers were Sidney's next-door neighbor, Jessica Bowden, and Marco Davis, a supervisor at a psychiatric hospital. Neither character played a big role in the narrative; their motivations felt unbelievable, and the mystery fell flat. This problem existed long before Scream 7, as well-regarded entries like Scream 6 also had forgettable killers who didn't offer any of Stu and Billy's social commentary, tension, or impact.
Can Scream 8 Get Things Back to Basics?
While Scream 7 had its flaws , certain elements felt authentic to the original. For one thing, modern technology played a key role in the film's narrative. Technology's evolution has been important in the franchise ever since the Woodsboro police questioned Billy Loomis about why a teenager would need a "mobile telephone," and when Scream 2 used Caller ID. AI technology and its potential for abuse were key themes in Scream 7 , exploiting a very real fear audiences feel in 2026. Scream 7 didn't quite connect the dots as well as it could have, but clearly, the writers made an effort to keep the series grounded in the real world.
As a franchise, Scream is at its best when it has something to say, and when its killers have depth and nuance that makes them scary beyond their use of a sharp knife and a voice changer. The franchise has often lost sight of that, though exceptions like the excellent Scream 4 do exist. None of the Scream movies have been able to surpass the original's sheer brilliance, but the series has never hit the same lows as many other major horror franchises . There's just some room for improvement when it comes to its killers.
Paramount has already started early production on Scream 8 , which isn't surprising given the seventh film's massive box office success. Details about the next installment remain slim, but the filmmakers should look back to 1996's Scream to see what it did so well. 30 years after the original movie's release, no other killers in the series are on the same level as Billy Loomis and Stu Macher.
